documentNotes.title: Instructions
documentNotes.statement:
**Time**: 3 hours ($\sim 45$ minutes for Q1, $\sim 65$ minutes for Q2 and $\sim 70$ minutes for Q3).

**Questions**: All three questions should be attempted. Each question contains independent parts so that later parts can be attempted even if earlier parts are incomplete.

**Solutions**: Answers and calculations are to be written on loose paper **ON ONE SIDE ONLY**. Students should ensure their **name** and **school** is clearly written on the **first** answer sheet and that **all** pages are numbered. **EACH QUESTION ANSWERED must be started on a new page.** A standard formula booklet with standard physical constants may be used if desired.

**Instructions**: This paper will be invigilated over Zoom with all candidates starting at 9am, however please **do not discuss** any aspect of the paper on the internet until 9am Saturday 6$^{\mathrm{th}}$ March.

**Clarity**: Solutions must be written legibly, in black pen (the papers are scanned), and working down the page. Scribble will not be marked and overall clarity is an important aspect of this exam.

**Eligibility**: The International Olympiad will be held during November 2021; all sixth form students are eligible to participate.

**Calculators**: Any standard calculator may be used, but calculators cannot be programmable and must not have symbolic algebra capability.

---

**Training Dates and the IOAA** (Bogota, Colombia, November 2021)

*The team will be selected from Y12 students taking this paper* **as well as** *Y12 students taking the Senior Physics Challenge paper in March. The best students that are eligible to represent the UK at the IOAA will be invited to attend the* **Training Camp** *to be held online from* **(Tuesday 6$^{\mathrm{th}}$ April to Saturday 10$^{\mathrm{th}}$ April 2021)**. *Astronomy material will be covered; problem solving skills and observational skills (telescope and naked eye observations) will be developed. At the Training Camp a Data Analysis exam along with a Round 3 theory paper will be sat. A team of five students (plus one reserve) will be selected for further training, mostly done remotely with (hopefully) additional training camps in the summer.*

documentNotes.title: Important Formulae
documentNotes.statement:
You might find the diagram of an elliptical orbit below useful in solving some of the questions:

**Elements of an elliptic orbit**:

| | |
|---|---|
| $a = \mathbf{OA}\ (= \mathbf{OP})$ | semi-major axis |
| $b = \mathbf{OB}\ (= \mathbf{OC})$ | semi-minor axis |
| $e = \sqrt{1 - \frac{b^2}{a^2}}$ | eccentricity |
| $\mathbf{F}$ | focus |
| $\mathbf{PF} = a(1-e)$ | periapsis distance (shortest distance from $\mathbf{F}$) |
| $\mathbf{AF} = a(1+e)$ | apoapsis distance (longest distance from $\mathbf{F}$) |

**Kepler’s Third Law**: For an elliptical orbit, the square of the period, $T$, of an object about the focus is proportional to the cube of the semi-major axis, $a$ (as defined above), such that

$$T^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM}a^3\ ,$$

where $M$ is the total mass of the system (typically dominated by the central object) and $G$ is the universal gravitational constant.

**Vis-Viva Equation**: For an elliptical orbit, the speed $v$ of an object at a distance $r$ from the focus is related to the semi-major axis, $a$, total mass of the system, $M$, and universal gravitational constant, $G$, (as defined above), such that

$$v^2 = GM\left(\frac{2}{r} - \frac{1}{a}\right)\ .$$

**Magnitudes**: The apparent magnitudes of two objects, $m_1$ and $m_0$, are related to their apparent brightnesses, $b_1$ and $b_0$, via the formula

$$\frac{b_1}{b_0} = 10^{-0.4(m_1 - m_0)}\ .$$

The absolute magnitude of an object, $\mathcal{M}$, is the same as its apparent magnitude when viewed from 10 pc, hence the relationship between apparent and absolute magnitude and distance is

$$m - \mathcal{M} = 5\log\left(\frac{d}{10}\right)\ ,$$

where $d$ is measured in parsecs.

problems.title: Mercury’s Rotation Period with Aricebo
problems.statement:
In November 2020 the Aricebo Telescope at the National Astronomy and Ionosphere Centre (NAIC) in Puerto Rico was decommissioned due to safety concerns after extensive storm damage. First opened in November 1963, this brought an end to an illustrious contribution to radio astronomy where, with a dish diameter of 304.8 m (1000 ft), it was the largest radio telescope in the world until 2016. Its important discoveries range from detection of the first extrasolar planets around a pulsar to fast radio bursts, as well as a pivotal role in the search for extraterrestrial intelligence (SETI), however in this question we will explore its earliest major revelation: that Mercury was not tidally locked.

Mercury had already been studied with optical and infrared telescopes, however the advantage of a radio telescope was that you could send pulses and receive their reflections. This radar-ranging technique had already been used with Venus to measure the distance to it and hence provide the data necessary for a definitive measurement of an astronomical unit in metres.

The radar echo from Mercury is much harder to detect due to the extra distance travelled and its smaller cross-sectional area (its radius is $2440$ km). In April 1965, Pettengill and Dyce sent a series of $500$ µs pulses at $430$ MHz with a transmitted power of $2.0$ MW towards Mercury whilst it was at its closest point in its orbit to Earth. In ideal circumstances the beam would stay parallel, however diffraction widens the beam as shown on the right in Fig 1.

parts.label: a.
parts.statement: Calculate the power of each echo received by the Aricebo telescope and hence determine the total number of photons in each echo, given the echo was detected $579.3$ s after being transmitted and Mercury’s surface only reflects $6.5\%$ of the incident radio photons. Assume $\theta = 0.16^{\circ}$ and the reflected photons from Mercury are scattered randomly within only the hemisphere facing Earth.
parts.statementAfter:
The signal-to-noise ratio of this echo was high enough that Doppler broadening of the received signal was reliably detected, allowing a determination of the rotation rate of Mercury. In August 1965 the same scientists sent $100$ µs pulses and sampled the echo on short timescales as it returned. The strongest echo (received first) came from the point of the planet closest to the Earth (called the sub-radar point), with later echos coming from other parts of the surface in an annulus of increasing radius (see Fig 2).

Photons from the approaching side would be blueshifted to a higher frequency, whilst those from the receding side would be redshifted to a lower frequency. Hence, by measuring the Doppler shift and the time delay, you can map the rotational velocity as a function of apparent longitude and so can calculate the apparent rotation rate (as well as the direction of rotation and co-ordinates of the pole).

The Doppler shift with light is given as

$$\frac{\Delta f}{f} = \frac{v}{c}\ ,$$

where $\Delta f$ is the shift in frequency $f$, $v$ is the line-of-sight velocity of the emitting object and $c$ is the speed of light.

parts.label: b. (i)
parts.statement:
Averaging over a series of pulses from August 1965, after correcting for the relative motion of the Earth and Mercury and the rotation rate of the Earth during the observations, the difference between the frequencies of photons from the extreme left and right parts of an annulus received $500$ µs after the initial echo was $\Delta f_{\mathrm{total}} = 4.27$ Hz.

Given that the pulse was Doppler shifted twice (once when reflected, once again when received back at Aricebo) show that the rotational period of Mercury is $\sim 60$ days. Assume that the axis of rotation is normal to the plane of observations. [1 day = 24 hours]

parts.label: b. (ii)
parts.statement: Mercury has a semi-major axis of $0.387$ au. Rounding slightly if necessary, express the ratio orbital period : rotational period in a simple integer form (the integers should be $< 10$).
parts.statementAfter: Ever since the first maps of Mercury’s surface by Schiaparelli in the late 1880s, many in the scientific community believed that Mercury would be tidally locked and so always present the same hemisphere to the Sun. The reason they expected the rotational period to be the same as its orbital period (i.e. a $1:1$ ratio), rather like the Moon, is because it is so close to the Sun and the tidal torques causing this synchronicity are proportional to $r^{-6}$ where $r$ is the distance from the massive body. Given it is the closest planet to the Sun, it receives by far the largest torques, so the discovery it was in a different ratio was a complete surprise to many of the scientists at the time.

parts.label: c. (i)
parts.statement:
The eccentricity of the planet’s orbit became the prime suspect as to why its actual ratio would be stable over long time periods.

Calculate how many times larger the tidal torque is when Mercury is at perihelion than when it is at aphelion, given the eccentricity of the orbit is 0.206.

parts.label: c. (ii)
parts.statement: Assuming the tidal torque at perihelion is the dominating factor in setting Mercury’s rotation rate, predict the rotational period of Mercury if it were to behave as though it was tidally locked when passing through perihelion. Compare this to the measured value and comment on validity of the assumption.

answer.note: Similar to the measured value, so the assumption is valid (official solution).

parts.label: c. (iii)
parts.statement: Fig 3 shows the orientation of Mercury’s axis of minimum moment of inertia (the axis the tidal torque acts upon) if the ratio had been $1:1$. Redraw this diagram but for the ratio found in part b (ii). Assume the initial orientation at perihelion looks the same in both cases (so only the other five positions are needed, separated equally in time) and that the planet both orbits and rotates in an anticlockwise direction. [Note: the orientation when it returns to perihelion may not be the same as it was initially.]

answer.note: Drawing: the new axes alternate between vertical and horizontal, with ends a and b correctly labelled (official solution figure).

figures.caption: Figure 1: *Left*: The Aricebo telescope before it was damaged. Credit: NAIC. *Right*: When transmitting a pulse from a radio telescope, diffraction prevents the beam from staying perfectly parallel and so the width of the beam increases by $2\theta$. Credit: OpenStax, College Physics.
figures.alt: Left: aerial photograph of the Arecibo radio dish in a forested valley with its suspended receiver platform and support towers. Right: line drawing of a dish antenna of diameter D on a lattice tower, with the transmitted beam edges diverging from the dish rim by angle θ at top and bottom.

figures.caption: Figure 2: *Left*: Snapshots of the reflections of a single $100$ µs pulse. The strength of the echo weakens as you move to later delays (as represented by the scale factor in the top right of each snapshot) and hence you need to use an annulus rather than detections from the horizon. The small arrows indicate the Doppler shifted frequency associated with intersection of the annulus with the apparent equator for each delay. The horizontal axis is in cycles per second (and so 1 c/s = 1 Hz). Credit: Dyce, Pettengill and Shapiro (1967). *Top right*: The key principles of the delay-Doppler technique, looking at a cross-section of the planet. At the very centre is the sub-radar point (the point on the planet’s surface closest to the Earth). As you move away from the sub-radar point the light has to travel further before it can be reflected, and hence the echo from those regions arrives later. The brightest point of any given annulus is where it intersects the apparent equator (due to the largest reflecting area), and so in each of the snapshots that is why the extreme Doppler shifts are boosted relative to the middle. Credit: Shapiro (1967). *Bottom right*: The same as the snapshots, but this time summed over the first $500$ µs of reflections. Here the difference between the extreme left and right frequencies reliably detected is $\sim 5$ Hz, but when corrected for relative motion of the Earth and Mercury it becomes the value given in part c. Credit: Pettengill, Dyce and Campbell (1967).

Top right: disc of the planet with the projection of the apparent rotation axis (ω), apparent equator, approaching and receding edges, an annulus defined by time delay and two vertical strips defined by Doppler shift. Bottom right: "MERCURY SPECTRUM 17 AUG. 1965", echo power (0 to 1.0) versus frequency (c/s) from −3 to 4, peaked at 0.

solution.statement:
**Q1 – Mercury Rotation Period with Aricebo** **[25 marks]**

**a.** We can use the light travel time to get the distance to Mercury

$$d_{Merc} = c \times \frac{t_{Merc}}{2} = 3.00\times10^{8}\times\frac{579.3}{2} = 8.69\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m} \qquad [1]$$

From this we can work out the radius of the beam

$$r_{beam} = d_{Merc}\tan\theta = 8.69\times10^{10}\times\tan 0.16^{\circ} = 2.43\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m} \qquad [1]$$

[Accept $r_{beam} = d_{Merc}\tan\theta + R_{Aricebo}$ although the effect of $R_{Aricebo}$ is negligible as Mercury is so far away. Also accept small angle approximation if $\theta$ is correctly converted into radians]

Consequently the intensity of the beam at Mercury is then

$$b_{Merc} = \frac{P}{\pi r_{beam}^2} = \frac{2.0\times10^{6}}{\pi(2.43\times10^{8})^2} = 1.08\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}} \qquad [1]$$

This means the total power reflected is

$$P_{refl} = b_{Merc}\times\pi R_{Merc}^2\times0.065 = 1.08\times10^{-11}\times\pi(2440\times10^{3})^2\times0.065 = 13.1\ \mathrm{W} \qquad [1]$$

Treating it as a point source radiating in just the hemisphere that faces Earth

$$b_{Earth} = \frac{P_{refl}}{2\pi d_{Merc}^2} = \frac{13.1}{2\pi(8.69\times10^{10})^2} = 2.77\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{W\,m^{-2}} \qquad [1]$$

Consequently, the power received by Aricebo is

$$P_{received} = b_{Earth}\times\pi R_{Aricebo}^2 = 2.77\times10^{-22}\times\pi\left(\frac{304.8}{2}\right)^2 = \boxed{2.02\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{W}} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[6]}$$

Turning this into a number of photons:

$$E_{phot} = hf = 6.63\times10^{-34}\times430\times10^{6} = 2.85\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{J} \qquad [1]$$

$$n = \frac{E_{tot}}{E_{phot}} = \frac{P_{recieved}t_{pulse}}{E_{phot}} = \frac{2.02\times10^{-17}\times500\times10^{-6}}{2.85\times10^{-25}} = \boxed{35500\ \mathrm{photons}} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[2]}$$

[This drop in power of $10^{23}$ is why you need such a powerful transmitter and such a large receiving dish to pick up the echo, and hence why it was such a hard measurement to make at the time]

**b. i.**

Helpful diagram of the situation [1]

Calculating x from the path difference between a beam that reflects of the sub-radar point and the edge of the annulus:

$$x = c\times\frac{1}{2}t = 3.00\times10^{8}\times\frac{1}{2}\times500\times10^{-6} = 7.50\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m} \qquad [1]$$

We can now calculate α,

$$\cos\alpha = \frac{R-x}{R} = \frac{2440-75}{2440} = 0.969 \therefore \alpha = 14.2^{\circ} \qquad [1]$$

Using the Doppler effect equation given, with $\Delta f$ halved twice (once for the two journeys, once to compare from sub-radar point to edge rather than edge to edge),

$$v_{obs} = \frac{\frac{1}{4}\Delta f_{total}}{f}c = \frac{\frac{1}{4}\times4.27}{430\times10^{6}}\times3.00\times10^{8} = 0.745\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \qquad [1]$$

Considering the geometry of the situation to get the tangential (rotational) velocity,

$$v_{rot} = \frac{v_{obs}}{\sin\alpha} = \frac{0.745}{\sin 14.2^{\circ}} = 3.027\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \qquad [1]$$

$$\therefore T_{rot} = \frac{2\pi R_{Merc}}{v_{rot}} = \frac{2\pi\times2440\times10^{3}}{3.027} = 5.06\times10^{6}\ s = \boxed{58.6\ \mathrm{days}} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[6]}$$

[Students using $v_{rot} = \frac{\Delta f_{total}}{f}c = 2.98\ m\ s^{-1}$ to get $T_{rot} = 59.56$ days only get the final mark for ecf on their v$_{\mathrm{rot}}$ (i.e. 1 out of 6). T$_{\mathrm{rot}}$ can be given in seconds or days, but if in the former a comparison to 60 days must be made]

[We are fortunate that the rotational axis of mercury is almost perfectly normal to the plane of observations, so this is almost identical to the real rotational period]

**ii.** From Kepler’s third law,

$$T_{orb} = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi^2a^3}{GM_{\odot}}} = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi^2}{6.67\times10^{-11}\times1.99\times10^{30}}\times(0.387\times1.50\times10^{11})^3} = 7.63\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{s} = 88.28\ \mathrm{days} \qquad [1]\,[1]$$

We can now work out the ratio

$$\therefore \text{ratio} = \frac{T_{orb}}{T_{rot}} = \frac{88.2836}{58.617} = 1.506 \approx 1.5 \qquad \text{[allow ecf with } T_{rot} = 60 \text{ days]} \qquad [0.5]$$

$$\therefore \boxed{3:2} \qquad [0.5] \quad \mathbf{[3]}$$

**c. i.** Given $r_{peri} = a(1-e)$ and $r_{aph} = a(1+e)$ and $\tau \propto r^{-6}$

$$\therefore \frac{\tau_{peri}}{\tau_{aph}} = \left(\frac{r_{peri}}{r_{aph}}\right)^{-6} = \left(\frac{1-e}{1+e}\right)^{-6} = \left(\frac{1-0.206}{1+0.206}\right)^{-6} = \boxed{12.3} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[1]}$$

**ii.** Finding the perihelion distance first

$$r_{peri} = a(1-e) = (0.387\times1.50\times10^{11})(1-0.206) = 4.61\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m} \qquad [1]$$

[Give this mark if they have already calculated r$_{\mathrm{peri}}$ in c) i) instead]

Using the vis-viva equation given at the beginning of the paper,

$$v_{peri} = \sqrt{GM_{\odot}\left(\frac{2}{r_{peri}} - \frac{1}{a}\right)} = \sqrt{6.67\times10^{-11}\times1.99\times10^{30}\left(\frac{2}{4.61\times10^{10}} - \frac{1}{0.387\times1.50\times10^{11}}\right)} = 5.89\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}} \qquad [1]$$

Working out the orbital angular velocity,

$$\omega_{orb} = \frac{v_{peri}}{r_{peri}} = \frac{5.89\times10^{4}}{4.61\times10^{10}} = 1.28\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad\,s^{-1}} \qquad [1]$$

If $\omega_{orb} = \omega_{rot}$ [which gives $v_{rot} = 3.12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$]

$$\therefore T_{rot} = \frac{2\pi}{\omega_{rot}} = \frac{2\pi}{1.28\times10^{-6}} = 4.91\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{s} = \boxed{56.9\ \mathrm{days}} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[4]}$$

This is similar to the measured value of T$_{\mathrm{rot}}$ ∴ valid assumption [1] **[1]**

**iii.**

New axes are alternating vertical and horizontal lines [1] **[1]**

Ends for a & b correctly labelled [1] **[1]**

[This does mean that it needs two Mercurian years before the perihelion orientation is the same – as such one (solar) day on Mercury lasts two years!]

problems.title: Great Conjunctions and the Star of Bethlehem
problems.statement:
On 21$^{\mathrm{st}}$ December 2020, Jupiter and Saturn formed a true spectacle in the southwestern sky just after sunset in the UK, separated by only $0.102^{\circ}$. This is close enough that when viewed through a telescope both planets and their moons could be seen in the same field of view (see Fig 4).

When two planets occupy the same piece of sky it is known as a conjunction, and when it is Jupiter and Saturn it is known as a great conjunction (so named because they are the rarest of the naked-eye planet conjunctions). The reason it happens is because Jupiter’s orbital velocity is higher than Saturn’s and so as time goes on Jupiter catches up with and overtakes Saturn (at least as viewed from Earth), with the moment of overtaking corresponding to the conjunction. The process of the two getting closer and closer together has been seen in sky throughout the year (see Fig 5).

parts.label: a. (i)
parts.statement:
In ideal observing conditions the two planets are far enough apart that they should be (just about) distinguishable to the naked eye, however to some observers in imperfect conditions they would appear as a single bright dot, brighter than either planet on its own.

During the conjunction, the apparent magnitudes of Jupiter and Saturn were $m_J = -1.97$ and $m_S = 0.63$, respectively (ignoring dimming by the atmosphere). What would be the apparent magnitude of the two planets if they appeared to an observer as a single point? [Hint: it is not simply $-1.97 - 0.63 = -2.60$.]

parts.label: a. (ii)
parts.statement: Although they appeared close in angle, there was a very considerable distance between the two planets. At conjunction, Jupiter was $5.926$ au from Earth whilst Saturn was $10.827$ au (see Fig 5). If they were actually next to each other in space such that they could be treated as a single object, how far from the Earth (in au) would they need to be to have the same apparent magnitude as calculated in the previous part? For simplicity, assume that both planets can be modelled as (very low luminosity) stars so that the change in brightness is only due to changing the distance from the Earth (i.e. ignore the complications from the changing distance from the Sun affecting the number of reflected photons and the changing geometry affecting the illuminated fraction of the planet’s surface).
parts.statementAfter: The time between conjunctions is known as the synodic period. Although this period will change slightly from conjunction to conjunction due to different lines of perspective as viewed from Earth (see Fig 5), we can work out the *average* time between great conjunctions by considering both planets travelling on circular coplanar orbits and ignoring the position of the Earth.

parts.label: b. (i)
parts.statement:
Jupiter has a period of $4332.589$ days and Saturn has a period of $10\,759.22$ days (where $1$ day $= 24$ hours). Note: be careful as your calculations will be very sensitive to rounding errors.

Calculate the time between great conjunctions as viewed from the centre of the Solar System (this will be equal to the average synodic period). Give your answer in years (where $1$ year $= 365.25$ days). [Hint: consider a reference frame rotating at the same rate as Jupiter.]

parts.label: b. (ii)
parts.statement: Use your answer to predict the date (to the nearest day) of the next great conjunction.

parts.label: b. (iii)
parts.statement: Some astronomers have suggested that the ‘Star of Bethlehem’ seen by the magi (‘wise men’) on their way to Jesus’ birth was in fact a great conjunction. Use your average synodic period to find the date of the great conjunction in the first decade BC and give your answer to the nearest month. [Note: be careful with BC years as year 0 in your calculation is equivalent to 1 BC, since 31$^{\mathrm{st}}$ December 1 BC is followed by 1$^{\mathrm{st}}$ January 1 AD]
parts.statementAfter:
For circular coplanar orbits the centre of Jupiter’s disc would pass in front of the centre of Saturn’s disc every conjunction, and hence have an angular separation of $\theta = 0^{\circ}$ (it is measured from the centre of each disc). In practice, the planets follow elliptical orbits that are in planes inclined at different angles to each other.

Fig 6 shows how this affects the real values for over 8000 years’ worth of data, which along with different synodic periods between conjunctions makes it a difficult problem to solve precisely without a computer. However, after one synodic period Saturn has moved about $2/3$ of the way around its orbit, and so roughly every $3$ synodic periods it is in a similar part of the sky. Consequently every third great conjunction follows a reasonably regular pattern which can be fit with a sinusoidal function.

parts.label: c. (i)
parts.statement:
By empirically fitting a sinusoidal function (which is assumed to be the same for each track, just with a fixed phase difference between them) and assuming all conjunctions are separated by the average synodic period, we can give rough estimations for the separations of any given great conjunction. Note: be careful as your calculations will be very sensitive to rounding errors.

By reading off the graph, give an equation for Track A of the form $\theta = |D\sin(\frac{2\pi t}{\lambda} + \phi_A)|$, where $t$ is the (decimalised) date in years, and $D$, $\lambda$, and $-\pi/2 < \phi_A \leq \pi/2$ are values that need to be determined. [Hint: ensure your function passes through the 2020 data point, and the function is decreasing as it does.]

answer.note: D = 1.20° (allow 1.10°–1.30°), λ = 2500 years (allow ±300 years), φ_A = 1.12 rad (official marking scheme).

parts.label: c. (ii)
parts.statement: Without having to read anything else off the graph, write down the equations for Tracks B and C, given the same restrictions on $\phi_B$ and $\phi_C$.

parts.label: c. (iii)
parts.statement: State which track the ‘Star of Bethlehem’ great conjunction is on, and hence use the relevant equation to predict its separation. How does it compare to the 2020 great conjunction?

answer.value: Track A; θ ≈ 1.07°, much further apart than the 2020 great conjunction

parts.label: c. (iv)
parts.statement: When is the next great conjunction at least as close as the 2020 one (i.e. $\theta \leq 0.102^{\circ}$)? Give its year and the value of $\theta$.

parts.label: c. (v)
parts.statement: Similarly, when was the last great conjunction at least as close as the 2020 one? Give its year and the value of $\theta$.

parts.label: c. (vi)
parts.statement: Using your equations, calculate the probability that a great conjunction has $\theta \leq 0.102^{\circ}$.

answer.note: Values 5.00%–5.91% accepted within the allowed range of D (official marking scheme).

Credit: Robin Catchpole. *Right*: The view from Arizona on the day of the closest approach as viewed with the Lowell Discovery Telescope. Credit: Levine / Elbert / Bosh / Lowell Observatory.
figures.alt: Left: telescope image on a blue twilight sky labelled "16:30 UTC, 20 December 2020" showing Saturn with moons Rhea and Titan above, and Jupiter with Callisto, Ganymede, Io and Europa below, plus the star HD191250. Right: black-background telescope image with ringed Saturn at the top and banded Jupiter with faint moons at the bottom.

figures.caption: Figure 5: *Left*: Demonstrating how Jupiter and Saturn have been getting closer and closer together over the last few months. Separations are given in degrees and arcminutes ($1/60^{\mathrm{th}}$ of a degree). Credit: Pete Lawrence. *Right*: The positions of the Earth, Jupiter and Saturn that were responsible for the 2020 great conjunction. The precise timing of the apparent alignment is clearly sensitive to where Earth is in its orbit. Credit: *timeanddate.com*.
figures.alt: Left: composite over a sunset horizon of the positions of Saturn (left column) and Jupiter (right column) joined by lines on dates from 02 Oct 2020 (7° 19′) to 21 Dec 2020 (0° 06′), every five days. Right: diagram of orbits with Saturn, Jupiter, the Sun and Earth, a dashed line of sight from Earth through Jupiter to Saturn, labelled "Great Conjunction 2020".

figures.caption: Figure 6: *Top*: All great conjunctions from 1800 to 2300, calculated for the real celestial mechanics of the Solar System. We can see that each great conjunction belongs to one of three different series or tracks, with Track A indicated with orange circles, Track B with green squares, and Track C with blue triangles. *Bottom*: The same idea but extended over a much larger date range, up to 10 000 AD. It is clear the distinct series form broadly sinusoidal patterns which can be used with the average synodic period to give rough predictions for the separations of great conjunctions. The opacity of points is related to each conjunction’s angular separation from the Sun (where low opacity means close to the Sun, so it is harder for any observers to see). Credit: Nick Koukoufilippas, but inspired by the work of Steffen Thorsen and Graham Jones / Sky & Telescope.

Bottom: the same three tracks from about 1600 to 10000 (axis "Year"), separation 0.00 to 1.25, forming interleaved sinusoidal patterns with points of varying opacity.

solution.statement:
**Q2 – Great Conjunctions and the Star of Bethlehem** **[35 marks]**

**a. i.** Given that brightness adds linearly, given the brightness of Jupiter (b$_{\mathrm{J}}$) and of Saturn (b$_{\mathrm{S}}$), the joint brightness of Jupiter and Saturn b$_{\mathrm{J+S}}$ is

$$\frac{b_{J+S}}{b_S} = \frac{b_J + b_S}{b_S} = \frac{b_J}{b_S} + 1 \qquad [1]$$

Using the formula connecting magnitudes and brightness given at the start of the paper,

$$\frac{b_{J+S}}{b_S} = 10^{-0.4(m_{J+S} - m_S)} \therefore m_{J+S} = m_S - 2.5\log\left(\frac{b_J}{b_S} + 1\right)$$

$$= m_S - 2.5\log\left(10^{-0.4(m_J - m_S)} + 1\right) \qquad [1]$$

$$= 0.63 - 2.5\log\left(10^{-0.4(-1.97-0.63)} + 1\right) = \boxed{-2.06} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[3]}$$

[Coincidentally, $-\sqrt{(-1.97)^2 + (0.63)^2} = -2.068$ ; this approach receives 0 marks]

**ii.** To balance the magnitudes for being at the same distance, we can use absolute magnitudes given the formula at the beginning of the paper (with distances converted into pc)

$$\mathcal{M}_J = m_J - 5\log\left(\frac{d_J}{10}\right) = -1.97 - 5\log\left(\frac{5.926\times1.50\times10^{11}}{10\times3.09\times10^{16}}\right) = 25.7$$

Similarly, $\mathcal{M}_S = 27.0$ [need both absolute magnitudes for the mark] [1]

Using a similar approach to the previous part of the question to get the combined absolute magnitude,

$$\mathcal{M}_{J+S} = \mathcal{M}_S - 2.5\log\left(10^{-0.4(\mathcal{M}_J - \mathcal{M}_S)} + 1\right) = 27.0 - 2.5\log\left(10^{-0.4(25.7-27.0)} + 1\right) = 25.4 \qquad [1]$$

$$\therefore d_{J+S} = 10\ \mathrm{pc}\times10^{(m_{J+S} - \mathcal{M}_{J+S})/5} = 10\ \mathrm{pc}\times10^{(-2.06-25.4)/5} = 3.15\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{pc} = 9.72\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{m} = \boxed{6.48\ \mathrm{au}} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[3]}$$

[Must be in au for final mark. Make some allowance for high sensitivity to rounding errors]

[Even at a standardised distance, Jupiter is still considerably brighter. If we had kept it as reflected photons and thus had to take into account the change in incident radiation, we would get $d_{J+S} = 6.91$ au, showing that our simplifying approximation is reasonable]

**b. i.** Moving into a frame of reference where Jupiter is stationary,

$$\omega_{J+S} = \omega_J - \omega_S \therefore \frac{1}{T_{J+S}} = \frac{1}{T_J} - \frac{1}{T_S} \qquad [1]$$

$$\therefore T_{J+S} = \left(\frac{1}{4332.589} - \frac{1}{10759.22}\right)^{-1} = 7253.455\ \mathrm{days} = \boxed{19.86\ \mathrm{years}} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[2]}$$

[Must be in years for the final mark. First mark is for any sensible approach in terms of ω]

**ii.** Rewriting $T_{J+S}$ into something more convenient

$$T_{J+S} = 20\ \mathrm{years} - 51.545\ \mathrm{days}$$

∴ next conjunction 52 days before 21$^{\mathrm{st}}$ Dec [1]

52 days = 21 in Dec + 30 in Nov + 1 in Oct ∴ $\boxed{30^{\mathrm{th}}\ \mathrm{Oct}\ 2040}$ [2] **[3]**

[One mark for the year (2040), one for the date. Allow $\pm1$ day. Alternatively, some students may look for the 304$^{\mathrm{th}}$ day in 2040]

[The real date is 31$^{\mathrm{st}}$ Oct 2040 so this model has done remarkably well – due to the dependence on the Earth’s position in its orbit the gap between conjunctions can vary up to $\sim 320$ days above or below the average value]

**iii.** In 2020 years there have been $\frac{2020}{19.86} = 101.7$ cycles

∴ need 102 cycles before 2020 conjunction [1]

Start date = 10 days before the end of the year $= 2020 + \frac{356}{365.25} = 2020.975$ [1]

[Give this mark if they have already calculated a decimalised start date in b) ii) instead. The top of the fraction must be 356 as 2020 is a leap year – lose this mark for other values]

∴ end date $= 2020.975 - (102\times19.86) = -4.63$ [1]

0.63 years = 7.57 months before 31$^{\mathrm{st}}$ Dec ∴ May [1]

Since a number between 0 and 1 corresponds to 1 BC, between -1 and 0 corresponds to 2BC, and so on, ∴ a number between -5 and -4 corresponds to 6 BC ∴ $\boxed{\mathrm{May}\ 6\ \mathrm{BC}}$ [1] **[5]**

[One mark for the year (6BC), one for the month. Allow $\pm1$ month]

[From our data a more precise prediction is 230.4 days before 31$^{\mathrm{st}}$ Dec and so 14$^{\mathrm{th}}$ May 6 BC. The real great conjunction in that decade occurred on 3$^{\mathrm{rd}}$ June 6 BC, so is rather close to our predicted date. This is before the death of King Herod in 4 BC, as required to fit in with the story, but it would have been seen in the constellation of Pisces in the NNE, so is unlikely to have been a ‘star in the East’]

**c. i.** Reading off the graph the amplitude (D) and the period (λ) of the sine wave:

$D = 1.20^{\circ}$ [allow $1.10^{\circ} \leq D \leq 1.30^{\circ}$] [1] **[1]**

$\lambda = 2500$ years [allow $\pm300$ years] [1] **[1]**

[Throughout the rest of this question, propagate the student’s values accordingly]

*[Note: in reality D is set by the difference in the inclinations of Jupiter and Saturn’s orbits]*

For $\phi_A$ the required properties are:

Correct behaviour (i.e. function is decreasing as it passes through 2020) [1]

In the specified range (i.e. $-\pi/2 < \phi_A \leq \pi/2$) [1] **[2]**

*Guidance on awarding the marks for $\phi_A$:*

$\phi_A = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{0.102}{1.2}\right) - \frac{2\pi\times2020.975}{2500} = -4.99\ \mathrm{rad}\ (= -286.1^{\circ})$ — Not in right range, or right behaviour so 0 marks

$\phi_A = -4.99 + \pi = -1.85\ \mathrm{rad}\ (= -106.1^{\circ})$ — Not in right range, or right behaviour so 0 marks

$\phi_A = -4.99 + 2\pi = 1.29\ \mathrm{rad}\ (= 73.8^{\circ})$ — In right range, but not right behaviour so 1 mark

$\phi_A = \left(\pi - \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{0.102}{1.2}\right)\right) - \frac{2\pi\times2020.975}{2500} = -2.02\ \mathrm{rad}\ (= -115.9^{\circ})$ — Not in right range, but right behaviour so 1 mark

$\phi_A = -2.02 + \pi = \boxed{1.12\ \mathrm{rad}}\ (= 64.1^{\circ})$ — In right range and right behaviour so 2 marks

[So final formula is $\theta = \left|1.20\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{2500} + 1.12\right)\right|$, but do not penalise students for not writing this so long as their values of D, λ and $\phi_A$ are clear]

**ii.** D and λ remain the same [this can be implied by calculations in later parts] [1] **[1]**

The phase difference is $\pi/3$, the only extra consideration being staying in the required range

$\phi_B = \phi_A - \frac{2\pi}{3} = \boxed{-0.98\ \mathrm{rad}}\ (= -55.9^{\circ})$ [1] **[1]**

$$\theta = \left|1.20\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{2500} - 0.98\right)\right|$$

$\phi_C = \phi_A - \frac{\pi}{3} = \boxed{0.07\ \mathrm{rad}}\ (= 4.1^{\circ})$ [1] **[1]**

$$\theta = \left|1.20\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{2500} + 0.07\right)\right|$$

[If they go outside the required range e.g. $\phi_B = \phi_A + \frac{\pi}{3} = 2.17\ \mathrm{rad}\ (= 124.1^{\circ})$ then lose that mark, unless they have already been penalised in part i. for being outside the range (in which case allow full ecf) . As in the previous part, do not penalise students for not writing the equations in the form $\theta = \cdots$ so long as their values of D, λ and $\phi_A$ are clear]

**iii.** Want 102 cycles before 2020 great conjunction, and 102 is divisible by 3

∴ Track A [1] **[1]**

$$\therefore \theta = \left|1.20\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{2500} + 1.12\right)\right| = \left|1.20\sin\left(\frac{2\pi\times-4.63}{2500} + 1.12\right)\right| = \boxed{1.07^{\circ}} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[1]}$$

This is much further apart than the 2020 great conjunction [1] **[1]**

[Note: other tracks coincidentally give similar values of θ; award 0 marks if wrong track used]

[Since this separation is over 10 times larger than the 2020 great conjunction (the real separation was almost the same as in this model), this adds evidence to suggest it would not have been as spectacular in the sky (and certainly not close enough to look like a single star), so that particular great conjunction is probably not an explanation for the Star of Bethlehem]

**iv.** Rather than using brute force to find it, the graph suggests a good one to try is the next point after 2020 on Track A

$\therefore t = 2020.975 + (3\times19.86) = 2080.55 \quad \therefore \text{year} = \boxed{2080}$ [1] **[1]**

$\therefore \theta = \left|1.20\sin\left(\frac{2\pi\times2080.55}{2500} + 1.12\right)\right| = \boxed{0.078^{\circ}}$ (so good guess) [1] **[1]**

[Using intuition here saved us a lot of time. The real date is 15$^{\mathrm{th}}$ March 2080, and the real separation will actually be almost identical to the 2020 great conjunction]

**v.** Again, to avoid brute force, the graph suggests we see whether there is anything suitable around Track B’s last x-intecept

$$0 = 1.20\sin\left(\frac{2\pi t}{2500} - 0.98\right) \therefore t = \frac{2500\times0.98}{2\pi} = 388$$

These repeat every ½ λ so the last one was $388 + \frac{2500}{2} = 1638$ [1]

Looking at the number of track intervals you need to go back,

$n = \frac{(2020.975+19.86)-1638}{3\times19.86} = 6.76 \therefore$ try 7 intervals back from 2040 [1]

$\therefore t = (2020.975 + 19.86) - (7\times3\times19.86) = 1623.80 \quad \therefore \text{year} = \boxed{1623}$ [1] **[3]**

$\therefore \theta = \left|1.20\sin\left(\frac{2\pi\times(2020.975+19.86)}{2500} - 0.98\right)\right| = \boxed{0.043^{\circ}}$ (good guess) [1] **[1]**

[Another example of intuition saving us lots of time. We have added the 19.86 to the 2020.975 to move from Track A to Track B. The real one was on 16$^{\mathrm{th}}$ July 1623 (our model predicts 19$^{\mathrm{th}}$ October) and had a separation of 0.086°. Some closer separations do happen, including transits (where the disc of Jupiter overlaps with the disc of Saturn), the next of which are due to happen in 7541 and 8674, and occultations (where Jupiter completely blocks out Saturn) in 7541, 13340 and 13738. (Note: 7541 sees part of a sequence called a triple conjunction, where retrograde motion means that Jupiter and Saturn meet three times in a short period. The transit is in February and the occultation is in June)]

**vi.** We need to know for how long in each cycle the curve has a value below 0.102° and compare that to the length of each cycle to get the overall probability

Using the notation of the diagram above,

$$\text{probability} = \frac{x}{\lambda/4} \qquad [1]$$

We can ignore phase information as that will not affect the size of $x$, just the co-ordinates of its start and end points, and hence we can simplify the expression for $\theta$ to find $x$

$$0.102 = 1.20\sin\left(\frac{2\pi x}{2500}\right) \therefore x = \frac{2500}{2\pi}\times\sin^{-1}\left(\frac{0.102}{1.20}\right) = 33.86\ \mathrm{years} \qquad [1]$$

$$\therefore \text{prob} = \frac{33.86}{2500/4} = 0.0542 = \boxed{5.42\%} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[3]}$$

[Accept it given as either a decimal or a percentage. Note that λ cancels in the expression for probability so it is only dependent on their value of D, giving prob $= \frac{\sin^{-1}(0.102/D)}{\pi/2}$ ; this approach gains all the marks and gives values ranging from 5.00% to 5.91% in the allowed range of D. Allow any other sensible approaches that give results within this range]

[The real value (taken from the number of conjunctions satisfying this condition over 16000 years of conjunctions) is 5.34% (38 instances out of 711) showing how well this model does. The orbits of the planets change slightly over time due to their gravitational interactions, so extending this pattern arbitrarily far into the future or past is unlikely to give precise results]

figures.alt: Graph of θ = |D sin(2πt/λ)| (red curve) against t with a horizontal blue line at θ = 0.102°; purple vertical lines mark a zero of the curve, the point where the curve crosses 0.102° (separation x, double arrow below the axis) and the next maximum a quarter period λ/4 later (double arrow at top).

problems.title: High Resolution Stellar Photos
problems.statement:
The surface of the Sun has a temperature of $\sim 5700$ K yet the solar corona (a very faint region of plasma normally only visible from Earth during a solar eclipse) is considerably hotter at around $10^6$ K. The source of coronal heating is a mystery and so understanding how this might happen is one of several key science objectives of the Solar Orbiter spacecraft. It is equipped with an array of cameras and will take photos of the Sun from distances closer than ever before (other probes will go closer, but none of those have cameras).

Launched in February 2020 (and taken to be at aphelion at launch), it arrived at its first perihelion on 15$^{\mathrm{th}}$ June 2020 and has sent back some of the highest resolution images of the surface of the Sun (i.e. the base of the corona) we have ever seen. In them we have identified phenomena nicknamed as ‘campfires’ (see Fig 7) which are already being considered as a potential major contributor to the mechanism of coronal heating. Later on in its mission it will go in even closer, and so will take photos of the Sun in unprecedented detail.

parts.label: a. (i)
parts.statement:
When it reached first perihelion, radio signals from the probe took 446.58 s to reach Earth.

Show that the spacecraft’s perihelion is $\sim 0.5$ au, giving your answer to 4 s.f., and hence estimate the launch date, assuming the Earth’s orbit is circular. Note that 2020 is a leap year and take $1$ year $= 365.25$ days. [Hint: You may wish to use a numerical method.]

answer.note: Official scheme: 0.4998 au with the simple form of Kepler’s third law also gets full marks; 18 Feb also allowed.

parts.label: a. (ii)
parts.statement:
The circumference of an ellipse, unlike for a circle, has no closed form. A good approximation from Ramanujan (1914) is

$$C \approx \pi(a+b)\left[1 + \frac{3j^2}{10+\sqrt{4-3j^2}}\right] \quad , \text{ where } \quad j = \frac{a-b}{a+b}\ ,$$

and $a$ and $b$ represent the semi-major and semi-minor axes, respectively. Use this to work out the distance travelled by the probe between launch and perihelion to 4 s.f.

parts.label: a. (iii)
parts.statement:
The exact solution for the circumference is

$$C = 4a\int_0^{\pi/2}\sqrt{1 - e^2\sin^2 t}\ \mathrm{d}t\ ,$$

where $e$ is the eccentricity and $t$ is an angle in radians. The integral has no analytical solution, but can be written as an infinite series expansion and hence the expression becomes

$$C = 2a\pi[1 - De^2 - Ee^4 - \frac{5}{256}e^6 - \ldots]\ .$$

Find the values of $D$ and $E$, given as fractions in their simplest terms, and hence calculate a new value for the distance travelled by the probe (also to 4 s.f.). Compare this to the approximation in the previous part and comment on your answer.

*[A helpful infinite series expansion is $(1+x)^n = 1 + nx + \frac{n(n-1)}{2}x^2 + \frac{n(n-1)(n-2)}{6}x^3 + \ldots$]*
parts.statementAfter: The highest resolution photos are taken with the Extreme Ultraviolet Imager (EUI), which consists of three separate cameras. One of them, the Extreme Ultraviolet High Resolution Imager (HRI$_{\mathrm{EUV}}$), is designed to pick up an emission line from highly ionised atoms of iron in the corona. The iron being detected has lost 9 electrons (i.e. Fe$^{9+}$) though is called Fe X (‘ten’) by astronomers (as Fe I is the neutral atom). Its presence can be used to work out the temperature of the part of the corona being investigated by the instrument.

answer.value: D = 1/4, E = 3/64; distance travelled 2.281 au (same as the Ramanujan approximation to 4 s.f.)

parts.label: b. (i)
parts.statement:
The energy density of black-body radiation, $u$, at temperature $T$ is given as

$$u = \int_0^{\infty}\frac{8\pi h\nu^3}{c^3}\frac{1}{\exp(h\nu/k_{\mathrm{B}}T) - 1}\,\mathrm{d}\nu\ ,$$

and the number density of black-body radiation, $n$, at temperature $T$ is given as

$$n = 16\pi\zeta(3)\left(\frac{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}{hc}\right)^3\ .$$

Here $h$ is Planck’s constant, $\nu$ is the frequency, $c$ is the speed of light, $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is Boltzmann’s constant, and $\zeta$ is the Riemann zeta function for which $\zeta(3) \approx 1.202$.

The average energy per photon is given as $\bar{E} = \frac{u}{n} = \varepsilon k_{\mathrm{B}}T$. Find the numerical value of $\varepsilon$. *[Standard integral: $I = \int_0^{\infty}\frac{x^3}{\exp(x)-1}\,\mathrm{d}x = \frac{\pi^4}{15}$]*

parts.label: b. (ii)
parts.statement: Assuming the plasma of Fe ions is in thermal equilibrium with the photons, and that the average energy of the photons is equal to the ionisation energy of Fe X (which is $22\,540$ kJ mol$^{-1}$), calculate the temperature of the plasma. Give your answer to 4 s.f.
parts.statementAfter:
The photons detected by HRI$_{\mathrm{EUV}}$ are emitted by a rearrangement of the electrons in the Fe X ion, corresponding to a photon energy of $71.0372$ eV (where $1$ eV $= 1.60\times10^{-19}$ J). The HRI$_{\mathrm{EUV}}$ telescope has a $1000''$ by $1000''$ field of view (FOV, where $1^{\circ} = 3600'' = 3600$ arcseconds), an entrance pupil diameter of 47.4 mm, a couple of mirrors that give an effective focal length of 4187 mm, and the image is captured by a CCD with $2048$ by $2048$ pixels, each of which is $10$ by $10$ µm.

Although we are viewing the emissions of Fe X ions, the vast majority of the plasma in the corona is hydrogen and helium, and the bulk motions of this determine the timescales over which visible phenomena change. In particular, the speed of sound is very important if we do not want motion blur to affect our high resolution images, as this sets the limit on exposure times.

parts.label: c. (i)
parts.statement:
The Rayleigh criterion is

$$\theta = 1.22\frac{\lambda}{D}\ ,$$

where $\theta$ is the minimum angular diameter (in radians) that can be resolved by a telescope, $\lambda$ is the observing wavelength and $D$ is the diameter of the aperture of the telescope.
The speed of sound in a plasma is

$$v_s = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma k_B T}{\mu}}, \quad \text{for which} \quad \mu = \frac{m_p}{2X + 3Y/4 + Z/2}\ ,$$

where $\mu$ is the mean particle mass ($X$, $Y$, $Z$ are the mass fractions of hydrogen, helium and elements heavier than helium, respectively), $m_p$ is the mass of a proton, and $\gamma$ is the adiabatic ratio.

Determine the theoretical minimum angular diameter of an element resolvable by this optical system. Give your answer in arcseconds ($''$).

parts.label: c. (ii)
parts.statement: In practice, this is not achieved as the pixels are not small enough. Given that each picture element is spread across two pixels (in 1D) to allow adequate sampling, what is the actual minimum angle resolved on the CCD? Give your answer in arcseconds ($''$). [Hint: consider the geometry of the optical system and note that the angles are small enough that the small angle approximation can be used.]

parts.label: c. (iii)
parts.statement: Later on in its mission, Solar Orbiter will have a perihelion of 0.284 au. Calculate the physical size on the Sun (in km) of each picture element in an image taken with HRI$_{\mathrm{EUV}}$ as well as the FOV in units of $R_{\odot}$.

answer.value: 203 km per picture element; FOV 0.297 R☉ (by 0.297 R☉)

parts.label: c. (iv)
parts.statement: If the mass fractions of the surface of the Sun are $X = 0.7381$, $Y = 0.2485$, and $Z = 0.0134$, and treating the plasma as an ideal monatomic gas so that $\gamma = 5/3$, determine the speed of sound of the plasma (in km s$^{-1}$) at the base of the corona. Hence, by comparison to your answer from the previous part, estimate the upper limit on the length of an exposure to avoid motion blur in the plasma. You should ignore any motion blur from the relative motion of the spacecraft or the rotation of the Sun.

solution.statement:
**Q3 – High Resolution Stellar Photos** **[40 marks]**

**a. i.** This is a diagram of the situation (note: Earth and probe are orbiting anticlockwise)

Given the light travel time,

$$x = 446.58\times3.00\times10^{8} = 1.3397\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{m} = 0.8932\ \mathrm{au} \qquad [1]$$

Considering the geometry of the triangle Earth-Sun-Probe after travelling for time t:

$$x^2 = r_{peri}^2 + (1\ \mathrm{au})^2 - 2r_{peri}(1\ \mathrm{au})\cos\theta \qquad \text{[cosine rule]} \qquad [0.5]$$

$$\theta = \pi - \frac{2\pi t}{1\ \mathrm{year}} \qquad [0.5]$$

Keeping $r_{peri}$ in au, and given t is half the period of the probe’s orbit, T, we can use Kepler’s third law [= K3] to work out t in SI units:

$$a = \frac{1}{2}\left(1 + r_{peri}\right)(1\ \mathrm{au}) \text{ and } (2t)^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{GM_{\odot}}a^3$$

$$\therefore t = \sqrt{\frac{\pi^2}{8GM_{\odot}}\left((1.50\times10^{11})\left(1 + r_{peri}\right)\right)^3} \qquad [2]$$

Substituting this into our equations above to form one where $r_{peri}$ is the only unknown:

$$r_{peri}^2 + 1 - 2r_{peri}\cos\left(\pi - 2\pi\frac{\sqrt{\frac{\pi^2}{8GM_{\odot}}\left((1.50\times10^{11})\left(1+r_{peri}\right)\right)^3}}{365.25\times24\times60\times60}\right) - x^2 = 0 \qquad [1]$$

Using an appropriate numerical method, $r_{peri} = \boxed{0.4956\ \mathrm{au}}$ [2] **[7]**

[Allow any valid method to find the root of the equation such as Newton-Raphson starting with r$_{\mathrm{peri}}$ = 0.5 au, using a graphical calculator to find the roots, or even using trial and error (starting from 0.5 au). The final answer must be 4 s.f. otherwise a mark is dropped. If given in metres, a comparison must be made to 0.5 au (also in metres) to show they are approximately the same]

[If students use the ‘simple’ version of K3, $T^2 = a^3$, where $T$ is already in years and $a$ is already in au, then they will get $t = \sqrt{\frac{1}{32}\left(1 + r_{peri}\right)^3}$ so the equation to be solved is $r_{peri}^2 + 1 - 2r_{peri}\cos\left(\pi - 2\pi\sqrt{\frac{1}{32}\left(1 + r_{peri}\right)^3}\right) - x^2 = 0$, which gives $r_{peri} = \boxed{0.4998\ \mathrm{au}}$. This approach receives full marks (and is somewhat simpler to type into a calculator)]

Given we know $r_{peri}$, we can find $a$, $t$ and therefore the launch date:

$$a = \frac{r_{peri}+1}{2} = \frac{0.4956+1}{2} = 0.7478\ \mathrm{au} \qquad [1]$$

[This mark may be given in part (iii) instead if not awarded here]

$$\therefore t = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{4\pi^2}{GM_{\odot}}a^3} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\frac{4\pi^2}{6.67\times10^{-11}\times1.99\times10^{30}}(0.7478\times1.50\times10^{11})^3} \qquad [1]$$

$$= 1.0244\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s} = 118.567\ \mathrm{days} \qquad [1]$$

So we need 15$^{\mathrm{th}}$ June – 118.567 days

118.567 days = 15 in June + 31 in May + 30 in April + 31 in March + 11.567 in Feb

so will be 29 – 11.567 = 17.433 ∴ $\boxed{17^{\mathrm{th}}\ \mathrm{Feb}}$ [allow 18$^{\mathrm{th}}$ Feb] [1] **[4]**

[Using the ‘simple’ version of K3 gives a = 0.7499 au, t = 118.592 days, and the same launch date. This is effectively the same as if students use the r$_{\mathrm{peri}}$ = 0.5 au given, although doing that with the SI version of K3 gives t = 119.090 days and so 16$^{\mathrm{th}}$ Feb. Using the given r$_{\mathrm{peri}}$ and the simple version of K3 gives t = 118.618 days. A launch date of 17$^{\mathrm{th}}$ Feb corresponds to arriving at perihelion at 00:00 on 15$^{\mathrm{th}}$ June, whilst 18$^{\mathrm{th}}$ Feb allows for students presuming a later time of arrival (up to 23:59 on 15$^{\mathrm{th}}$ June). Allow ecf on the launch date from their own values of t]

[In reality, the probe reached a perihelion distance of 0.514 au and was launched on 10$^{\mathrm{th}}$ Feb. The reason for the discrepancy is that the Earth’s orbit is elliptical and reaches perihelion on 4$^{\mathrm{th}}$ Jan so the probe was not actually at aphelion at launch (although it did reach it on 17$^{\mathrm{th}}$ Feb), and the aphelion distance was 0.986 au]

**ii.** Using the equations given at the beginning of the paper,

$$r_{peri} = a(1-e) \therefore e = 1 - \frac{r_{peri}}{a} = 1 - \frac{0.4956}{0.7478} = 0.3372 \qquad [1]$$

$$e = \sqrt{1 - \frac{b^2}{a^2}} \therefore b = a\sqrt{1-e^2} = 0.4956\sqrt{1-0.3372^2} = 0.7040\ \mathrm{au} \qquad [1]$$

$$\therefore j = \frac{a-b}{a+b} = \frac{0.7478-0.7040}{0.7478+0.7040} = 0.030176 \qquad [1]$$

$$\therefore C = \pi(a+b)\left[1 + \frac{3j^2}{10+\sqrt{4-3j^2}}\right] = \pi(0.7478+0.7040)\left[1 + \frac{3(0.030176)^2}{10+\sqrt{4-3(0.030176)^2}}\right] = 4.562\ \mathrm{au} \qquad [0.5]$$

But only half an ellipse has been covered, so distance travelled $= \boxed{2.281\ \mathrm{au}}$ [0.5] **[4]**

[Must be 4 s.f. for the final mark. Carrying forward values from the ‘simple’ version of K3 gives e = 0.3335, b = 0.7070 au, j = 0.02947, C = 4.578 au and so distance travelled is 2.289 au (essentially the same as if using the given r$_{\mathrm{peri}}$)]

**iii.** Using the given formula for a binomial expansion,

$$\begin{aligned} I &= \int_0^{\pi/2}(1 - e^2\sin^2 t)^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &= \int_0^{\pi/2} 1 + \frac{1}{2}(-e^2\sin^2 t) + \frac{\frac{1}{2}\left(-\frac{1}{2}\right)}{2}(-e^2\sin^2 t)^2 + \cdots\,\mathrm{d}t \\ &= \int_0^{\pi/2} 1 - \frac{1}{2}e^2\sin^2 t - \frac{1}{8}e^4\sin^4 t\,\mathrm{d}t \qquad \text{[correctly simplified expansion]}\ [1] \\ &= \int_0^{\pi/2} 1\,\mathrm{d}t - \frac{1}{2}e^2\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2 t\,\mathrm{d}t - \frac{1}{8}e^4\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^4 t\,\mathrm{d}t \end{aligned}$$

The first term is very easy to evaluate (and is effectively already given),

$$\int_0^{\pi/2} 1\,\mathrm{d}t = [t]_0^{\pi/2} = \frac{\pi}{2}$$

To do the other integrals we need to use the trig identities:

$$\sin^2 x = \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\cos 2x \text{ and } \cos^2 x = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\cos 2x$$

The second term,

$$\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^2 t\,\mathrm{d}t = \int_0^{\pi/2}\left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\cos 2t\right)\mathrm{d}t = \left[\frac{1}{2}t - \frac{1}{4}\sin 2t\right]_0^{\pi/2} = \frac{\pi}{4} \qquad [1]$$

The third term,

$$\begin{aligned} &\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^4 t\,dt \\ &= \int_0^{\pi/2}\left(\frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2}\cos 2t\right)^2 dt \\ &= \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\cos 2t + \frac{1}{4}\cos^2 2t\,dt \\ &= \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{1}{4} - \frac{1}{2}\cos 2t + \frac{1}{4}\left(\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}\cos 4t\right)dt \\ &= \int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{3}{8} - \frac{1}{2}\cos 2t + \frac{1}{8}\cos 4t\,dt \\ &= \left[\frac{3}{8}t - \frac{1}{4}\sin 2t + \frac{1}{32}\sin 4t\right]_0^{\pi/2} = \frac{3\pi}{16} \qquad [3] \end{aligned}$$

So putting back into our original formulae,

$$C = 4aI = 4a\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{1}{2}e^2\left[\frac{\pi}{4}\right] - \frac{1}{8}e^4\left[\frac{3\pi}{16}\right] - \cdots\right) = 2\pi a\left[1 - \frac{1}{4}e^2 - \frac{3}{64}e^4 - \cdots\right]$$

$$\therefore \boxed{D = \frac{1}{4}} \text{ and } \boxed{E = \frac{3}{64}} \qquad \text{[one mark for each correct fraction]} \qquad [2] \quad \mathbf{[7]}$$

We can now evaluate C numerically,

$$\begin{aligned} C &\approx 2\pi a\left[1 - \frac{1}{4}e^2 - \frac{3}{64}e^4 - \frac{5}{256}e^6\right] \\ &= 2\pi(0.7478)\left[1 - \frac{1}{4}(0.3372)^2 - \frac{3}{64}(0.3372)^4 - \frac{5}{256}(0.3372)^6\right] \\ &= 4.562\ \mathrm{au} \qquad [0.5] \end{aligned}$$

$$\therefore \text{distance travelled} = \boxed{2.281\ \mathrm{au}} \qquad [0.5] \quad \mathbf{[1]}$$

To 4 s.f., this is the same as the Ramanujan approximation (so very good!) [1] **[1]**

[Must be 4 s.f. for the final mark. If students forget the e$^{6}$ term, they will still get the same answer to 4 s.f. – do not penalise them for that mistake. Using the ‘simple’ version of K3 gives 2.289 au, again the same as before. The real difference between the two values is $4.5\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{au} = 680\ \mathrm{km}$, which is remarkably close]

[In reality, the distance the probe had travelled from launch to perihelion was 2.393 au, however the main reason for the discrepancy is the extra week of travel between launch and aphelion]

**b. i.** To get the integral to look like the standard one, we need to use a substitution:

Use $x = \frac{h\nu}{k_BT} \therefore \nu = \frac{k_BT}{h}x \therefore \mathrm{d}\nu = \frac{k_BT}{h}\mathrm{d}x$ [need correct dν for mark] [1]

Substituting this into the original integral,

$$u = \int_0^{\infty}\frac{8\pi h\nu^3}{c^3}\frac{1}{\exp\left(\frac{h\nu}{k_BT}\right)-1}d\nu = \int_0^{\infty}\frac{8\pi h}{c^3}\left(\frac{k_BT}{h}\right)^3\frac{x^3}{\exp(x)-1}\frac{k_BT}{h}dx \qquad [1]$$

$$= \frac{8\pi h}{c^3}\left(\frac{k_BT}{h}\right)^4\left[\frac{\pi^4}{15}\right] = \frac{8}{15}\pi^5\left(\frac{k_BT}{hc}\right)^3k_BT \qquad [1]$$

$$\therefore \bar{E} = \frac{u}{n} = \frac{\frac{8}{15}\pi^5\left(\frac{k_BT}{hc}\right)^3k_BT}{16\pi\left(\frac{k_BT}{hc}\right)^3\zeta(3)} = \frac{\pi^4}{30\zeta(3)}k_BT \qquad [1]$$

$$\therefore \varepsilon = \frac{\pi^4}{30\zeta(3)} = \boxed{2.701} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[5]}$$

[Third mark is for some attempt at simplification of the algebraic expression. No s.f. requirement in this question but expect at least 2 s.f. (and should really use 4 s.f. in the next part of the question). If get dν = dx and hence a value of ε that still has a value of T in it this is considered a major error and there is no ecf]

**ii.** Converting the ionisation energy into an energy of each photon

$$\bar{E} = \frac{22540\times10^{3}}{N_A} = \frac{22540\times10^{3}}{6.02\times10^{23}} = 3.744\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{J} \qquad [1]$$

$$\therefore T = \frac{\bar{E}}{\varepsilon k_B} = \frac{3.744\times10^{-17}}{2.701\times1.38\times10^{-23}} = \boxed{1.004\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{K}} \qquad \text{[must be 4 s.f.]} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[2]}$$

[Despite the considerable simplifications we have made to our model, this is remarkably close to the real value of temperature for which Fe X is the dominant fraction. In reality, it forms an equilibrium over a range of temperatures (contributing a detectable fraction from about 10$^{5.4}$ to 10$^{6.4}$ K) with various other ions in ionisation equilibrium – all you can compute is the ionic fraction at a given temperature (i.e. the plasma is never purely one ion)]

**c. i.** First, we can work out the wavelength given the photon energy,

$$E = \frac{hc}{\lambda} \therefore \lambda = \frac{hc}{E} = \frac{6.63\times10^{-34}\times3.00\times10^{8}}{71.0372\times1.60\times10^{-19}} = 1.75\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m} \qquad [1]$$

$$\therefore \theta = 1.22\frac{\lambda}{D} = 1.22\times\frac{1.75\times10^{-8}}{47.4\times10^{-3}} = 4.50\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{rad} = \boxed{0.0929''} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[2]}$$

[Must be in arcseconds for the final mark]

[Given the wavelength investigated is 17.5 nm, it is clearly in the extreme UV]

**ii.** Considering the geometry of the situation:

where s is the distance on the CCD and f is the focal length. Using the small angle approx:

$$\tan\theta \approx \theta = \frac{s}{f} \qquad [1]$$

$$\therefore \theta = \frac{2\times10\times10^{-6}}{4187\times10^{-3}} = 4.78\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad} = \boxed{0.985''} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[2]}$$

[Must be in arcseconds for the final mark. If only done for s = 1 pixel (i.e. 10 µm), lose 1 mark. Another valid approach for the first mark is to use the formula for the plate scale, $\frac{\theta}{s} = \frac{1}{f} = 0.239\ \mathrm{rad\,m^{-1}} = 2.39\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{rad\,pixel^{-1}} = 0.493''\ \mathrm{pixel^{-1}}$]

**iii.** Using similar geometry to the previous part of the question,

where d is the distance on the Sun and r is the distance to the Sun. Using the small angle approximation again,

$$d \approx r\theta = (0.284\times1.50\times10^{11})\times4.78\times10^{-6} = \boxed{203\ \mathrm{km}} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[1]}$$

Considering the field of view (FOV) of the telescope, we need to convert 1000” into rad

$$FOV = r\theta = (0.284\times1.50\times10^{11})\times\left(\frac{1000}{3600}\times\frac{\pi}{180}\right) = 2.07\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m} = \boxed{0.297\ R_{\odot}} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[1]}$$

[So the field of view is 0.297 R$_{\odot}$ by 0.297 R$_{\odot}$. First answer must be in km and second in R$_{\odot}$ for the marks]

[Originally the mission plan was to go even closer, however it was adjusted to have a minimum perihelion of $> 0.28$ au so that the solar panel technology could be reused from the BepiColombo mission, which will enter an orbit around Mercury in December 2025. Mercury’s perihelion is ≈ 0.30 au so Solar Orbiter will pass fully inside the orbit of Mercury. The minimum perihelion for Solar Orbiter will be on 7$^{\mathrm{th}}$ Feb 2027]

**iv.** Using the given mass fractions and formulae, plus the temperature from b. (ii)

$$\mu = \frac{m_p}{2X + \frac{3Y}{4} + \frac{Z}{2}} = \frac{m_p}{2(0.7381) + \frac{3(0.2485)}{4} + \frac{0.0134}{2}} = 0.599m_p = 1.00\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg} \qquad [1]$$

$$\therefore v_s = \sqrt{\frac{\gamma k_BT}{\mu}} = \sqrt{\frac{\frac{5}{3}\times1.38\times10^{-23}\times1.004\times10^{6}}{1.00\times10^{-27}}} = \boxed{152\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}}} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[2]}$$

[Must be in km s$^{-1}$ for the final mark. If students did not get a value for T from part b. they should have seen in the opening paragraph of the question that typical corona temperatures are 10$^{6}$ K and used that – penalise those that use the temperate of the surface of the Sun]

By comparing to the physical size of each picture element,

$$t = \frac{d}{v_s} = \frac{203}{152} = \boxed{1.34\ \mathrm{s}} \qquad [1] \quad \mathbf{[1]}$$

[The HRI$_{\mathrm{EUV}}$ will take images of 1 second exposure (with shorter exposure times in subfields of the FOV) every second in the ‘Discovery’ program, however most images will have a 2 second exposure with the interval time between images varying from seconds to minutes depending on the different observation programs]
